hints: Think about what causes the small M+1 peak when the molecule contains only C, H and O, and recall the natural abundance of 13C (about 1.1%).
Set up the relationship: % of M+1 relative to M equals number of C atoms multiplied by 1.1, then solve using 0.7/22.1.
walkthrough:
See where the M+1 peak comes from**
Picture your molecules flying through the mass spectrometer. Almost all carbon is $^{12}\text{C}$, but about 1.1% is $^{13}\text{C}$. If just one of the carbons in a molecule is $^{13}\text{C}$ instead of $^{12}\text{C}$, the mass is one unit heavier. That is your M+1 peak, so its size tells you how many carbons are present.

Turn the peak heights into a calculation**
First find M+1 as a percentage of M: $$(0.7/22.1) \times 100$$ Each carbon contributes about 1.1% to this value, so divide by 1.1: $$n(\text{C}) = \frac{0.7}{22.1} \times \frac{100}{1.1} \approx 2.88$$ You cannot have a fraction of an atom, so round to the nearest whole number, 3 carbon atoms.

Final answer: number of C = (0.7/22.1) x (100/1.1) = 2.88
= 3 carbon atoms

hints: Use Mr = 90 and subtract the mass of 3 carbons to find the mass left for H and O, then fit H and O to make 90.
walkthrough:
Build the formula from the mass left over**
You know $M_r = 90$ and there are 3 carbons. Carbons account for $3 \times 12 = 36$, leaving $90 - 36 = 54$ for H and O. Try oxygens: $3 \times 16 = 48$ leaves $6$ for hydrogen, giving $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$. That fits perfectly and uses only C, H and O with all C-C single bonds possible.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$ ($3 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 + 3 \times 16 = 90$)

hints: Recall the characteristic broad O-H regions: alcohol O-H around 3200-3600 cm-1 and carboxylic acid O-H as a very broad band around 2500-3000 cm-1.
Recall where a C=O stretch appears and which functional group must be present if you see both a very broad O-H and a C=O together.
walkthrough:
Sort the two different O-H bands**
Both 3350 and 2680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ are O-H stretches, but their shapes tell them apart. A broad strong band at 3350 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is the classic hydrogen bonded alcohol $\text{O-H}$. The very broad strong band centred near 2680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, sitting on top of C-H, is diagnostic for the $\text{O-H}$ of a carboxylic acid, $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

Add the carbonyl to confirm the acid**
A strong sharp absorption at 1725 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C=O}$ stretching. Together with the very broad O-H, this confirms a carboxylic acid group. So F contains both an alcohol $\text{ROH}$ and a carboxylic acid $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

Final answer: 3350 cm-1 broad and strong: $\text{O-H}$ bond, alcohol
2680 cm-1 very broad and strong: $\text{O-H}$ bond, carboxylic acid
1725 cm-1 strong: $\text{C=O}$ bond, carboxylic acid

hints: Add up the total H from C3H6O3 and use the integration ratio to check that the four areas must sum to 6H.
Place the most shielded alkyl signal near delta 1.4 and the most deshielded acid OH near delta 11-13.
Remember that a proton on carbon attached to oxygen is deshielded to about delta 3.5-4.5, while an alcohol OH typically appears around delta 2-5.
Match each shift to the Data Booklet ranges for CH next to O, alcohol OH and carboxylic acid OH, then assign areas 3:1:1:1.
walkthrough:
Use the total proton count to anchor integration**
From $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$ you have 6 protons in total. The spectrum shows four signals, so the areas must add to 6. The tall doublet at delta 1.4 is three times larger than the others, giving a 3:1:1:1 pattern. That immediately suggests a $\text{CH}_{3}$ group plus three different single protons.

Assign the two ends of the spectrum**
At delta 1.4 you are in the normal alkane region, so this is alkyl $\text{-CH}_{3}$ next to a CH. At the other extreme, delta 12.9 is highly deshielded and can only be the proton of $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$, a carboxylic acid OH, area 1.

Place the middle two signals**
Delta 3.9 is downfield for a C-H, which tells you that carbon is bonded to an electronegative oxygen atom, so $\text{-OCH}$, here a $\text{CH}$ bonded to OH, area 1. Delta 4.7 lies in the alcohol $\text{-OH}$ range, area 1. This gives two OH type protons plus one O-CH proton plus one CH3 group, exactly matching an alcohol plus a carboxylic acid.

Final answer: delta 1.4: alkyl $\text{-CH}_{3}$ / $\text{-CH}_{2}$ / $\text{-CH}$, area 3
delta 3.9: $\text{-OCH}$ / $\text{CH}$ next to O / electronegative atom, area 1
delta 4.7: alcohol $\text{-OH}$, area 1
delta 12.9: carboxylic acid $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$, area 1

hints: Look at the shape of the delta 1.4 signal in the spectrum and count the lines, then apply the n+1 rule to deduce neighbours.
walkthrough:
Read the splitting with the n+1 rule**
Zoom in on delta 1.4 and you see two closely spaced lines, a doublet. Splitting follows $n+1$, where $n$ is the number of equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon. A doublet means $n = 1$, so the $\text{CH}_{3}$ is next to a $\text{CH}$ bearing one proton.
Final answer: doublet, due to 1 proton on the adjacent / neighbouring carbon (n+1 = 2)

hints: Recall which protons exchange with D2O and disappear from the proton NMR spectrum.
walkthrough:
Spot the exchangeable protons**
$\text{O-H}$ protons are labile and exchange with deuterium in $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$: $\text{ROH} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{ROD} + \text{HOD}$. Deuterium does not show in proton NMR, so those signals vanish. That is the alcohol OH at delta 4.7 and the acid OH at delta 12.9.
Final answer: absorptions at delta 4.7 and 12.9 (alcohol $\text{-OH}$ and carboxylic acid $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$) absent

hints: Join the fragments CH3, CH bonded to O, alcohol OH and CO2H so that all C-C bonds are single and the formula is C3H6O3.
walkthrough:
Piece the fragments into one molecule**
You have $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{CH}$, that $\text{CH}$ attached to $\text{OH}$, and a $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ group. Linking them with single C-C bonds gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CH(OH)-C(=O)-OH}$. Check: 3 carbons, 6 hydrogens, 3 oxygens, contains one alcohol and one carboxylic acid, exactly as IR and NMR require.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CH(OH)-C(=O)-OH}$, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid

hints: Draw a seven membered ring and place two C=C double bonds in two different relative positions to make two distinct isomers.
walkthrough:
Place two double bonds in the seven ring**
Keep the seven sided skeleton and draw two double lines for $\text{C=C}$. For one isomer put them separated by one single bond, the 1,3 arrangement with conjugated double bonds. For the other put them separated by two single bonds, the 1,4 arrangement with isolated double bonds. Both have formula $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{10}$ and are positional isomers.
Final answer: P = cyclohepta-1,3-diene and Q = cyclohepta-1,4-diene (or vice versa): seven-membered rings each with two C=C bonds in different positions, e.g. conjugated vs isolated

hints: Count chemically distinct carbon environments by looking for a plane of symmetry through the seven membered ring in each diene.
Remember that each pair of symmetry equivalent carbons gives one peak, and alkene carbons are distinct from alkane CH2 carbons.
walkthrough:
Find symmetry in P**
Take the 1,3-diene. It has a plane of symmetry that pairs up carbons on either side of the ring. The four alkene carbons form two equivalent pairs, and the three $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons include one pair plus one unique carbon. That gives $2 + 2 = 4$ distinct carbon environments, so 4 peaks in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR.

Find symmetry in Q**
Take the 1,4-diene. It also has a plane of symmetry through the ring. Again the alkene carbons pair up and the $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups pair up leaving one unique $\text{CH}_{2}$, giving 4 distinct environments in total. So Q also shows 4 peaks.

Final answer: P: 4 peaks
Q: 4 peaks
